Temporal causal feature selection for robust machine learning modelling of
data center operations

Department of Information Systems, Paderborn University, Paderborn, Germany

A B S T R A C T
Modern data centers are complex, energy-intensive systems whose efficient operation is critical for the energy
transition. This paper introduces the TempCaFe (Temporal Causal Features) framework, which applies causal
feature selection to improve predictive modelling and intervention analysis in data center environments. By
integrating causal discovery with domain knowledge for time-series data, the approach not only improves the
predictive performance of machine learning models but also their robustness and interpretability. We evaluate
the utility of the proposed framework by training and evaluating 4026 models for 31 prediction tasks with
data from a data center simulation, a physical testbed, and two operational data centers with distinct cooling
architectures (air and water). The results indicate that causal feature selection, compared to traditional feature
selection methods, enhances prediction accuracy, especially after system interventions. Furthermore, models
trained with causal features require less than one-third of the original features and exhibit greater robustness to
data scarcity (number of samples). These findings highlight the potential of causal machine learning to enable
robust modelling of data center operations and provide a foundation for decision-making tasks such as what-if
analysis and the design of control systems.
1 . Introduction
Data centers (DCs) are at the heart of our digital infrastructure, as
they, for example, enable advancements in connectivity, cloud com­
puting, and artificial intelligence [1,2]. In 2016, DCs consumed an
estimated 200 TWh of electricity, comparable to South Africa’s annual
energy use [3]. Projections for 2030 suggest that DC electricity demand
could double or even triple, reaching levels comparable to those pro­
jected for the entire African continent [4,5]. Consequently, reducing

the energy consumption and carbon emissions of DCs is critical for
improving their environmental sustainability.
Improving DC operations requires accurate digital representations
of these systems in the form of models or digital twins. These rep­
resentations enable the evaluation of key operational scenarios, such
as analyzing the effects of modifying temperature setpoints and their
impact on energy consumption, and serve as the basis for advanced
optimization frameworks, including model predictive control [6,7] and
reinforcement learning [8,9]. By leveraging these intelligent control sys­
tems, operators can enhance the efficiency and sustainability of DCs,
particularly in energy-related areas such as thermal energy manage­
ment, heat recovery, and the direct energy consumption of IT and
cooling systems.
DC modelling strategies generally fall into three main categories:
simplified physics-based models, computational fluid dynamics/heat
transfer (CFD/HT) simulations, and data-driven techniques [10].
Simplified physics-based approaches are computationally efficient but
rely on strong and restrictive assumptions that can hinder real-world
applicability [11]. At the other end of the spectrum, CFD/HT tech­
niques involve numerically solving detailed physical equations, leading
to highly accurate and fine-grained predictions, though this comes at
the cost of being computationally heavy and requiring significant setup
effort [10,12].
In recent years, data-driven models have gained traction as a more
efficient and accurate alternative to conventional simulation-based tech­
niques [13]. They are used to model from operational data a response
variable of the system, such as energy consumption, based on one or
more input variables, like IT load or weather conditions. However, these
models typically rely exclusively on statistical associations, limiting their
capacity to generalize beyond the conditions observed during training
[14–16]. This limitation becomes especially critical when assessing the
impact of targeted interventions, such as shifts in IT workload or control
system setpoints [12].
The challenges of data-driven modelling arise from using a “kitchen
sink” approach to machine learning (ML), which assumes that more
data necessarily leads to more accurate predictions, while neglecting
theory-grounded causal mechanisms [17–20]. In response, scholars have
called for integrative approaches that combine the explanatory power
of causal inference with the predictive strengths of modern ML algo­
rithms [17]. A prominent framework that embodies this synthesis is
causal machine learning (causal ML) [21,22]. Data-driven predictive
models rely exclusively on correlations; that is, they minimize fore­
casting error based on statistical associations, making them vulnerable
to issues such as spurious correlations and structural biases (e.g., con­
founding or collider bias). In contrast, causal ML seeks to model the
underlying causal mechanisms that generate the data, aiming to identify
cause-and-effect relationships [14]. Because causal mechanisms remain
invariant under interventions, models that incorporate them generalize
more effectively beyond the training distribution [15]. To accomplish
this, causal ML merges methodologies from causal inference with the
flexibility of ML techniques. This enables decision-making grounded in
causal understanding rather than only on statistical associations.
In this regard, this work applies causal machine learning to im­
prove the energy-related modelling of data center operations. Its scope
includes:
1. We propose the TempCaFe framework for feature selection based
on automated causal discovery techniques for time-series data,
combined with the refinement of causal graphs through domain
knowledge. In addition, we explicitly account for temporal depen­
dencies (i.e., the selection of time lags). We propose an algorithm
to perform this integration seamlessly.
2. We benchmark the proposed framework against multiple tradi­
tional feature selection methods, evaluating their performance
in combination with a range of ML algorithms and different lag
selection strategies.
3. We train 4026 ML models and conduct extensive numerical ex­
periments across 31 prediction tasks, using datasets from two
controlled environments (a simulation and a physical testbed) as
well as from two real-world data centers covering both air-cooled
and water-cooled designs.
4. We assess the strengths and limitations of the proposed approach
in two distinct settings: prediction across the complete test set
and prediction after system interventions, providing insights into
the robustness and generalizability of the approach.
5. We analyze the proposed methods under varying amounts of
training data and conduct ablation and sensitivity analyses to
provide insights into robustness and data efficiency.
We found that causal feature selection methods informed by domain
knowledge improve the predictive accuracy of ML models for data center
operations. In particular, they are significantly more accurate in predict­
ing the effects of interventions than traditional feature selection methods
or models using all available features. In addition, models built with
causal features exhibit higher learning efficiency, as they require sub­
stantially fewer features for training and their performance degrades
less as the amount of training data is reduced.
Our study extends the existing literature on energy-related mod­
elling of DC operations for both traditional forecasting and scenarios
involving interventions. It contributes to research on causal ML in time
series [23,24] and integrating domain knowledge into the feature se­
lection process [25,26]. Furthermore, ML models trained with causal

2 . Background
2.1 . Causal machine learning and causal feature selection
There are two generally equivalent frameworks in causality: the
Potential Outcomes Framework, often referred to as the Neyman–Rubin
causal model [28], and Structural Causal Models (SCMs), pioneered by
Judea Pearl [21]. In the Potential Outcomes Framework, the causal
effect is conceptualized as the contrast between two hypothetical sce­
narios: the outcome of an intervention (𝑌(1)) versus the outcome under
a baseline or non-intervention scenario (𝑌(0)). This framework is widely
used in the social sciences and medicine to estimate causal effects. SCMs,
on the other hand, use Graphical Causal Models (GCMs) and structural
equations to represent how variables influence one another, aiming to
model the causal mechanisms of the data-generating process explicitly.
In this work, we represent the underlying causal structure of DC energy
systems using graphical models and therefore focus on the Structural
Causal Model (SCM) framework.
In a GCM, nodes represent variables and arrows between nodes rep­
resent causal relationships. A directed link from one node to another
designates the originating node as the parent and the receiving node as
the child. The combination of nodes and links follows distinct structural
patterns. One fundamental configuration is the chain, in which all ar­
rows point in the same direction, as shown in Fig. 1(a). In this setup, 𝑋
and 𝑍 are conditionally independent given 𝑌 (𝑋⟂⟂𝑍∣𝑌), with 𝑌 acting
as a mediator. Conditioning on 𝑌, for example, by fixing its value, ef­
fectively blocks the causal pathway from 𝑋 to 𝑍. Another key structure
is the fork, illustrated in Fig. 1(b), which represents a common cause.
Here, 𝑌 and 𝑍 become conditionally independent once 𝑋 is known
(𝑍⟂⟂𝑌∣𝑋), and 𝑋 serves as a confounder that introduces a spurious
correlation between 𝑌 and 𝑍. Adjusting for 𝑋 removes this non-causal
association. The third archetype is the collider, depicted in Fig. 1(c),
where two arrows converge on a common effect. In this configuration,
𝑋 and 𝑌 are marginally independent (𝑋⟂⟂𝑌), but conditioning on 𝑍
induces a spurious correlation between them, a phenomenon known as
collider bias [14].
Although chains, forks, and colliders can be combined into more
complex causal structures involving many variables, the underlying

GCMs support a wide range of causal tasks, including identifying causal
relationships, estimating causal effects, performing root-cause analysis,
and making causal predictions [29,30].
DC operations are typically represented as time series, where vari­
ables such as IT load and temperatures are tracked over time. In this
context, the causal graph has to represent the dynamics of the system
and account for causal effects across subsequent time steps, referred to as
lags. Fig. 2(a) illustrates this using a summary causal graph [31], where
nodes represent variables, edges denote causal relationships, and numer­
ical annotations on the links indicate the time lag of each causal effect.
A lag of 1 directly beneath a node signifies that the variable influences
itself in the future.
Causal graphs are acyclic, with causal effects unfolding repeatedly
over time. To make this temporal structure more explicit, Fig. 2(b) de­
picts a time-series graph in which each variable is expanded across
successive lags. In these graphs, a feature is defined as a combination
of a variable (e.g., 𝑋, 𝑌, or 𝑍) and a temporal lag (e.g., 𝑡−1, 𝑡−2).
These graphs can be used to select features for data-driven modelling,
effectively using causality as a feature selection approach. For instance,
when predicting 𝑌 at time 𝑡, we identify all direct causes of 𝑌 at time
𝑡 from the time-series graph in Fig. 2(b). Fig. 3(a) shows an example of
the causally relevant features, shown in green, that directly influence a
target variable, shown in blue. In contrast, a standard time-series pre­
diction without causal feature selection would typically include all six
available features shown in Fig. 3(b).
Once the relevant causal features have been identified, ML algo­
rithms can be applied to model the functional form of the relationships
between a target variable and its direct causes [21,32]. Restricting the
features of an ML model to direct causes promises to reduce statisti­
cal biases and improve both the accuracy and robustness of predic­
tions [33,33,34]. It of course also limits the number of overall features,
thereby lowering the computational cost and decreasing the likelihood
of overfitting [35,36].

2.2 . Causal discovery algorithms for time-series data
A GCM can be constructed either manually through expert domain
knowledge or by applying causal discovery algorithms. Causal discov­
ery (CD) refers to the process of automatically inferring a causal graph
from observational data. Several families of algorithms have been devel­
oped for this purpose [37,38]. Constraint-based approaches, such as the
Peter-Clark (PC) algorithm, rely on testing for conditional independence
between variables to infer the causal structure [39]. Score-based meth­
ods evaluate candidate graphs using scoring functions like the Bayesian
Information Criterion (BIC) or Minimum Description Length (MDL),
with Greedy Equivalence Search being a widely used algorithm in this
category [40]. Gradient-based techniques treat the search for a causal
graph as a continuous optimization problem; a notable example is the
NOTEARS algorithm [41]. Finally, functional discovery methods, such
as the Non-Gaussian Acyclic Model (LiNGAM), leverage independent
component analysis to model variables as functions of other variables
and noise [42].
The above-mentioned algorithms all focus on cross-sectional data,
but various adaptations for time-series data exist:
• PC1: a time-series variant of the PC algorithm performs indepen­
dence tests on the most relevant lagged variables and converges to
a small set of relevant causal parents [43].
• PCMCI: the Peter-Clark Momentary Conditional Independence al­
gorithm starts with the (PC1) algorithm by testing conditional
independence (Step 1) and MCI for addressing the autocorrelation
in the time series by testing conditional independence at specific
lags (Step 2). PCMCI allows conditioning only on relevant features
and has greater detection power [43].
• VARLiNGAM: a method that combines vector autoregressive
(VAR) modelling with the LiNGAM framework. The VAR compo­
nent accounts for lagged (temporal) dependencies, ensuring that
the influence of past values on current observations is modeled
explicitly. After removing these temporal effects, LiNGAM is ap­
plied to the residuals to identify instantaneous (contemporaneous)
causal relationships between variables. Identification (e.g., de­
termination of the causal effect) is achieved by exploiting the
non-Gaussianity of the innovations (or error terms/residuals), en­
abling the recovery of causal directions between the variables
[44–47].
• Dynotears: an extension of the NOTEARS algorithm tailored for
dynamic causal discovery in time-series data, using the concept of
score-based structure learning with temporal constraints. It solves
an optimization problem to estimate a dynamic Bayesian net­
work or temporal DAG by enforcing acyclicity and using sparsity-
inducing penalties [48].
Causal discovery algorithms for time-series data are based on sev­
eral assumptions. The causal Markov condition posits that a variable
is conditionally independent of all non-descendant variables given its
direct causes. Causal sufficiency assumes that all relevant causal vari­
ables are observed, thereby excluding hidden confounders. The causal
stationarity assumption requires that the causal relationships remain
stable over time.
In real-world applications, these assumptions are often difficult or
impossible to verify and are frequently violated, which can result in mis­
leading causal conclusions, either by detecting spurious relationships or
overlooking true causal dependencies [24,37,49,50]. The severity of this
issue depends on the specific causal task: it is particularly problematic
for causal effect estimation, while causal predictions tend to be more ro­
bust against violations [36]. Nevertheless, even in predictive settings,
spurious causal links can increase model sensitivity to distributional
shifts [23]. It is important to clarify that when we refer to “causal fea­
tures”, whether identified through causal discovery or through domain
knowledge, we do not claim to have recovered the true causal variables,
as the underlying data-generating process of a real-world DC remains
unknown. Rather, we treat these features as informed approximations
of causally relevant variables. These approximations can offer practi­
cal benefits by reducing bias and mitigating the influence of spurious
correlations in the data-driven modelling process.
2.3 . Prior work in ML modelling of data center operations and causal
machine learning applications
In recent years, ML approaches have been increasingly adopted for
predictive modelling of key DC metrics such as energy demand, heat
distribution, workload fluctuations, and operating costs. For instance,
power forecasting techniques have been analyzed, highlighting that
accurate prediction models are fundamental for reliable energy and ther­
mal management [51]. The authors reported that linear and polynomial
regression showed strong performance in estimating server power con­
sumption, but also stressed the importance of developing models that
reflect the interdependencies between thermal conditions and energy
use. Extending this line of work, researchers have examined hybrid
ensemble and modified neural network designs and showed that they
achieve higher robustness when addressing heterogeneous workloads
[52]. With respect to temperature forecasting, tree-based algorithms
such as LightGBM and XGBoost have been shown to outperform other
ML approaches in predicting airflow cooling behavior [53].
Despite their strong predictive performance in stable environments,
current ML approaches exhibit important limitations. Most models
are purely observational, with prediction error minimization as their
primary optimization goal. Consequently, they tend to capture statis­
tical associations without explicitly accounting for the data-generating
process or underlying causal dependencies [21,54]. This reliance on cor­
relations limits their robustness for tasks beyond standard prediction and
reduces their ability to accurately estimate the effects of interventions
on physical systems, thereby constraining their usefulness for decision-
making. Additionally, studies frequently include all available variables
in the prediction task, which often results in very high-dimensional input
spaces, making models more susceptible to the curse of dimensionality
and substantially increasing training complexity and computation time
for training and prediction.
Causal ML is increasingly being applied in domains such as medicine
[55,56], econometrics [57], and weather [35]. For example, focusing on
causal feature selection, Ganesh et al. [35] investigated the prediction of
Western Pacific tropical storm intensity using causal discovery methods.
Their approach treats causal discovery as a feature selection mecha­
nism that discards predictors that are (conditionally) independent of the
target given other variables, thus contributing no additional predictive
value. The study found that causal discovery achieved the most effective
trade-off between model simplicity and predictive performance, outper­
forming approaches that rely on all available features or other feature
selection techniques.
In the energy domain, there are applications of causal ML based
on the Potential Outcome Framework. For instance, Massidda and
Marrocu [58] introduced an energy forecasting approach for residen­
tial communities that combines Quantile Regression with causal ML

Previous studies have advanced the application of machine learn­
ing in data center environments and contributed to the emerging field
of causal machine learning. Building on these foundations, our work
extends the literature. We formalize and propose novel methods for
the integration of domain knowledge into time-series causal graphs,
including a practical algorithm to support this integration. We introduce
strategies for feature selection, lag specification, and evaluating multiple
causal discovery methods. We systematically compare the proposed ap­
proaches with traditional feature selection techniques and models that
use all available features. We include the most important causal discov­
ery techniques from the literature and state-of-the-art ML algorithms.
We also analyze time-series ML algorithms and their combination with
causal discovery methods. Furthermore, our study employs a compre­
hensive experimental design using both simulated and real-world data
from data centers, reflecting common facility data characteristics and
modelling targets with a focus on the energy domain. The experiments
are conducted at a large scale with 31 prediction tasks, 15 datasets,
empirical validation, robustness analysis, and data ablation studies.
Overall, this study expands the literature on modelling data-center op­
erations and causality, highlights the advantages of causally informed
modelling in complex data center systems, and offers contributions with
practical relevance for both researchers and practitioners.
3 . The TempCaFe framework
Fig. 4 provides an overview of our proposed TempCaFe (Temporal
Causal Features) framework. It combines causal discovery and domain
knowledge for selecting an optimal set of predictor variables and time
lags as features for training ML algorithms. The framework is structured
into five sequential phases.
The first phase consists of two parallel steps: preparing the dataset,
i.e., splitting it into training and test sets, and identifying relevant
domain knowledge about the physical system under investigation.
The second phase involves two activities. On one side, we apply
causal discovery algorithms to the training data to obtain a time-series
DAG that captures potential cause-and-effect relationships among the
variables of the dataset, including time lags. On the other side, a static
DAG is constructed based on the domain knowledge about the physical
system under study. While it may be theoretically possible to manually

In the third phase, potential variables or features (i.e., combinations
of variables and time lags) are systematically derived from the DAGs cre­

for feature selection: (1) only features derived from the time-series DAG
created through causal discovery (CD); (2) features identified from the
CD-generated time-series DAG, augmented with missing variables from
the domain-knowledge static DAG (DK&CDV); (3) variables derived
from the domain-knowledge static DAG enriched with time lags derived
from the causal discovery-generated time-series DAG (DK&CDL); and
(4) only variables derived from the domain-knowledge static DAG (DK)
with all available lags. Finally, we add any missing time-lag informa­
tion for DK&CDV and DK&CDL that was not previously identified as
significant in the causal discovery process (see Section 3.1 for details).
In the fourth phase, we select the final features with two strategies.
The first uses only the specific lags identified in the previous phase
(select lag). The second includes any variable with at least one de­
tected causal link and adds all of its lags (all lags). This second option is
included because precise lag selection may not be essential for ML per­
formance, and providing all lags for a causal variable might still yield
strong results.
It is important to note that some feature selection methods are com­
patible with only one lag-selection strategy. The DK approach uses only
the all lags strategy, since its feature selection step contains no lag
information, only variables identified by the domain knowledge. The
DK&CDL method uses only the select lag strategy, because its all lags
version would be identical to DK.
Lastly, in the fifth step, we train and evaluate different machine
learning algorithms on each of the final feature sets.
3.1 . Combination of causal discovery with domain knowledge
In this subsection, we explain how a DAG originating from causal dis­
covery can be integrated with domain knowledge by deletion or addition
of variables and lags.
Unlike editing a static causal graph that does not consider time [25],
the challenge of causality in time series also entails identifying the ap­
propriate time lags of when this causal relationship happens in time
[60]. Since these temporal dependencies are often difficult or impossi­
ble to infer solely from domain knowledge, we propose an approach that
combines causal discovery algorithms with domain knowledge insights
to guide the selection of relevant variables and lags. The pseudocode for
this procedure is presented in Algorithm 1, which produces two resulting
causal graphs.
The algorithm takes a DAG created through causal discovery 𝐺CD as
input, which contains combinations of variables and their lags, and a
DAG derived manually from domain knowledge 𝐺DK. The graph from
domain knowledge does not include variable–lag combinations; it only
contains the variables that are presumed to have a causal effect on the
target variable.

the statistical scores or measures used to infer causal dependencies. In

In dynamical physical systems, different interactions unfold on differ­
ent time scales. Some effects become observable within the next sampled
time step, while others manifest only after several subsequent steps. To
capture both types of temporal dependencies in a data-driven model, we
include these past time steps, referred to as lags.
To initiate the modelling process, it is necessary to select a maximum
lag as the temporal window considered during feature selection and
downstream ML modelling. This should be guided by the domain knowl­
edge of the complex physical system or based on significant correlations
in the data [62].
In this regard, we compute the partial correlations between vari­
ables in each dataset to identify the average lag at which the correlation
reaches its peak, beyond which the statistical association between vari­
ables decreases, and therefore this lag can be used as the maximum lag
[63].
In our experiments, we evaluate multiple datasets and sampling
resolutions. To select a common maximum lag across all settings, we
compute the maximum partial correlation for each dataset and take
the median of these values, which yields an effective maximum lag of
approximately 4.33, meaning 5 complete lags.
Furthermore, because in DC and control-system settings the strongest
causal effects typically influence the target variable within only a
few subsequent time steps, we consider five time steps a reasonable

3.4 . Datasets
We use datasets from four distinct sources to capture a compre­
hensive range of DC configurations commonly referenced in academic
literature and practical applications. These sources are a simulated air-
cooled data center (Sim), a water-cooled data center testbed (MiniDC), a
real-world water-cooled data center (DC1), and a real-world air-cooled
data center (DC2). Together, these datasets cover a wide range of oper­
ational conditions and cooling strategies. Comprehensive datasets and
variable descriptions for each DC are presented in Appendix (A-D),
alongside system schematics and static causal graphs derived from
domain knowledge.
An intervention in a dataset corresponds to a change in the control
system, such as adjusting the air temperature setpoint of the server room
or opening a valve that regulates cooling, either in a water-cooled rack
or in the Computer Room Air Handler (CRAH) unit of an air-cooled data
center. In the Sim and MiniDC, we manually control these interventions,
whereas in the two real data centers (DC1 and DC2), they are executed
autonomously by the control systems (see details in Appendix A-D).
Each dataset differs in terms of the number of observations, sampling
resolution, dataset size, targets, predictors, and interventional variables.
This reflects the heterogeneity of DC environments and modelling chal­
lenges. A summary of the key characteristics of each dataset is presented
in Table 3.
For the evaluation, we employ a time-series modelling using histor­
ical values of the variables across five time lags. This means that each
variable is expanded into five temporal features, corresponding to its
values at previous lags. Consequently, the total number of features used
in the modelling is determined by multiplying the number of original
variables by the number of five lags.
The prediction targets were selected to cover a broad range of vari­
ables relevant to modelling data center operations. In the Sim, the targets
are the air temperature in the server room and the energy consumption
of IT equipment. In the MiniDC testbed, the target is the water temper­
ature of the cooling loop, used as a proxy for heat recovery. For DC1,
the targets consist of four water temperatures associated with cooling
different racks. For DC2, the targets are the inlet and outlet air temper­
atures of the CRAH units in Appendices server room (see more details
in the Appendix A-D).
A prediction task is defined by combining a target and a dataset,
resulting in a total of 31. For each task, we apply both evaluation ap­
proaches, the complete test set evaluation and the after-intervention
evaluation.

may continue to propagate over several subsequent time steps until

5 . Discussion
In this article, we propose the TempCaFe framework, which com­
bines automated causal discovery with human domain knowledge for
feature selection. Unlike prior frameworks that focus primarily on static
systems [25], TempCaFe explicitly models dynamical systems. In addi­
tion, it extends existing work that focused on regression models [26] and
demonstrates how causal feature selection can be effectively combined
with time-series models by using lag-selection strategies. Furthermore,
the framework extends existing work that uses causal discovery as a fea­
ture selection method [26,35], as well as studies that edit the causal
graph with domain knowledge [60], through novel approaches to com­
bine automated causal discovery results and domain knowledge graphs
(DK, DK&CDL, and DK&CDV), along with a practical algorithm for their
integration.
In extensive experiments, we compared the predictive performance
of 4026 ML models trained on feature sets produced by this framework
with traditional feature selection methods and the use of all features
available. We evaluated the approaches with several time-series datasets
from the operations of four data centers. In the following, we discuss our

5.1 . Main contributions
Causal feature selection enhances model performance for pre­
diction tasks.
Tasks such as predicting the effects of IT-load changes, managing
temperatures, and reducing energy consumption are essential for opti­
mizing data-center operations. Several approaches in the literature have
focused on using ML algorithms for such tasks [51–53]. Existing stud­
ies are almost exclusively based on purely data-driven methods, but—as
we argued in this article—considering cause-and-effect relationships in
ML models is essential to avoid the pitfalls of purely correlation-based
approaches [14,16].
Although the reliability of causal discovery methods depends on
theoretical assumptions that are difficult to verify in real-world applica­
tions [35,36], our empirical findings show that causal features identified
through automated causal discovery or domain knowledge, or a combi­
nation of both, consistently yielded the best predictive accuracy across
all metrics, clearly outperforming the use of all available features and
traditional feature selection methods. The reason is that non-causal fea­
tures exhibit strong correlation with the target and act as redundant or
noisy proxies for latent system states, but are not true drivers of the tar­
get’s outcome. Hence, removing them yields models that better reflect

Regarding the selection of an optimal number of time lags, we ob­
served that in the pure prediction task, the time-series models performed
particularly well under the all lags strategy. A plausible explanation is
that the exact timing of causal effects (i.e., the precise lag) is less critical
for standard prediction tasks, and modern time-series architectures can
efficiently process large sets of lagged inputs. Even if some of these lags
are non-causal, the models can still extract useful predictive power from
them.
Causal feature selection significantly enhances model perfor­
mance for predictions after interventions.
Besides predictions in steady conditions, we also assessed how well
different methods perform when making predictions after interventions
in the system. This is crucial for moving from passive predictions to
active prescriptions, such as what-if analysis, and for designing control
systems in data centers. It has been argued that, in this context, purely
data-driven methods may be insufficient and causal reasoning becomes
essential [21,54].

The best model consisted of combining domain knowledge with
variables and lags identified by automated causal discovery methods.
The resulting causal features drastically outperformed those feature sets
generated by traditional feature selection methods, which were not con­
siderably better than the baseline of using all available features. This
underscores the importance of causality in intervention scenarios and in
tasks that extend beyond standard forecasting. Conditioning on causally
relevant lagged features preserves the invariance of predictive relation­
ships across operating regimes, making the resulting models far more
robust to distribution shifts induced by interventions.
Also, the results indicate that while using all lags is suitable for
standard predictions, it is inadequate for post-intervention forecasting,
where select lag clearly performs best. This emphasizes that accurately
predicting intervention effects requires capturing the detailed tempo­
ral dynamics of the system’s underlying causal structure, including
when effects occur and how the lags between variables relate to one
another.
Models trained with causal features can learn more efficiently
from data.
Our study shows that models using causal features identified through
TempCaFe experience substantially less performance degradation as
training set sizes decrease. The underlying theoretical reason is that they
rely on genuinely informative signals about the true data-generating
process rather than noisy proxies chosen by correlation-based methods.
The robustness of models built on causal features is highly relevant
for decision-making, what-if analysis, and control systems, where inter­
ventions are important but occur infrequently, resulting in datasets that
are sparse in terms of interventional data.
Furthermore, the superior performance in both evaluations and un­
der reduced data availability is achieved with high model parsimony.
The framework relies, on average, on less than one-third of the avail­
able features, which reduces the computational effort required for ML
training. While other feature selection methods may yield similarly sized
feature sets, they result in less trustworthy and less reliable predictions.
Ultimately, these results substantiate that improved performance
does not stem simply from maximizing variables and data volume, but
rather from the precise selection of the right features.
The combination of causal discovery with domain knowledge
improves the interpretability of the resulting ML models.
Integrating domain knowledge with causal discovery algorithms can
be challenging, as it often requires manual refinement of the causal
graph. A particular difficulty arises in lag selection: domain experts may
know that two variables are causally related, but not the precise tim­
ing of the effect [60]. Our framework addresses this issue by enabling
a seamless combination of causal graphs derived from algorithms with
those informed by domain expertise.
Additionally, the comparatively small number of selected causal
features—whose relevance is more readily recognizable by domain
experts—enables a reduced feature set that supports simpler and more
accurate interpretation of the final ML models.
Furthermore, causal discovery methods can automatically uncover
causal relationships in physical systems, while domain-knowledge
graphs encode the assumptions and the understanding provided by hu­
man knowledge about the physical system. Neither approach on its own
is guaranteed to produce a complete or fully accurate causal graph, but
combining them yields a robust representation. These hybrid graphs sup­
port more effective reasoning about the physical system and make the
assumptions underlying the ML modelling explicit, while achieving the
best predictive performance.
5.2 . Practical implications
In applied settings for modelling data center operations, our results
indicate that practitioners and data center operators should avoid simply
using all available features or relying solely on traditional feature se­
lection methods. Instead, causal discovery methods should be combined
with domain knowledge. The TempCaFe framework outlines a blueprint
for how to do this.
For forecasting tasks, the best approach is to use time-series mod­
els coupled with causally selected variables and all lags. When domain
knowledge about the physical structure of the data center is readily
available, it should be incorporated. When such knowledge is uncer­
tain or incomplete, causal discovery methods on their own still perform
well.
For tasks that extend beyond standard prediction, such as forecasting
under interventions, what-if analysis, or using ML models as a basis for
control, it is especially important to combine domain knowledge with
insights obtained from causal discovery and to rely on the select lags
strategy. Also, regression-based algorithms should be favored over time-
series methods, as they allow explicit selection of variables and their
precise lag effects.
Moreover, we recommend explicitly modelling the domain knowl­
edge in the form of causal graphs and combining it with automated
causal discovery. This approach enables data center operators to gain
deeper insights into the physical system, uncover previously unknown
causal relationships, and explicitly encode domain assumptions in the
modelling process.
Additionally, it is encouraged to use models trained on causal fea­
tures because they tend to be more robust when data is scarce. This is
particularly important in data center applications, where interventions
are limited or costly to perform (e.g., changing setpoints for server room
temperature).
Related to this, the proposed models typically also require fewer fea­
tures for training, reducing training time. This is a particularly important
advantage when datasets are large, the number of features is high, or
models need to be frequently retrained over time.
Overall, for practical applications in data centers, our results suggest
that using the proposed framework leads to ML models that are more
efficient, robust, require less training time, are more interpretable, have
better performance, and are suited for tasks beyond prediction.
5.3 . Limitations and future work
The performance of causal discovery methods can vary significantly
depending on the assumptions made about the dataset, the specific
method chosen, and the selection of hyperparameters. In our study,
we focused on four established methods from the literature, applying
their recommended hyperparameter settings, such as p-value thresh­
olds. We also conducted a sensitivity analysis of the PCMCI algorithm
with different parameters and one ML algorithm in Appendix F, showing
that changes in their alpha values affect prediction performance. Hence,
future work could explore a broader range of hyperparameter config­
urations and identify features that consistently appear across multiple
hyperparameter settings. This could lead to improved performance in
models built on causal discovery methods.
Also, the choice of the maximum lag can affect the feature selection
and the performance of the subsequent ML models. We selected a max­
imum lag of 5 based on statistical associations, domain knowledge of
data-center dynamics, and practical constraints related to computational
performance and real-world applicability. Nonetheless, using fewer or
more lags, for instance, to evaluate the impact of daily cycles on the
target variables, may affect both the feature-selection methods and the
resulting ML models. Future work could explore this by running experi­
ments on a single dataset, fewer methods, and low sampling resolution,
for instance, in hours, systematically varying the maximum lag to assess
its impact on feature selection and downstream model performance.
Furthermore, the interpretability of causal feature selection lies in
the fact that features provided by causal discovery with domain knowl­
edge are few and more aligned with the physical knowledge about the
system. However, we did not explicitly address the explainability of the
ML algorithms themselves once trained on these features. A promis­
ing avenue for future research would be to explain these models with

Moreover, our analysis of the intervention effects was conducted on
the time step after the interventions, as this is the point at which the
control systems in data centers are expected to exert their strongest influ­
ence. However, an intervention may not only have a causal effect on the
immediate next step after the intervention, but also on subsequent future
steps. Future work could address this limitation by proposing methods
to evaluate until which steps a causal effect is present, for instance, by
manually changing the interventional variables, and then training ML
algorithms to make multi-step predictions and evaluations.
In the manuscript, we introduced approaches that integrate domain
knowledge with causal discovery by first constructing a graph based
on domain knowledge of the system. We then used causal discovery
techniques to identify missing features or relevant lags. When the initial
human-defined graph contains inaccuracies, it can degrade the perfor­
mance of the overall approach, as shown in the Appendix G. Future work
could mitigate this risk by allowing for iterative refinement of the causal
graphs and potentially improving the downstream performance of ML
models trained on these features.
It is also important to clarify that while the scope of this study focused
primarily on causal prediction, other important tasks in causal infer­
ence, such as causal effect estimation, are also highly relevant. Future
research could extend the proposed framework by leveraging causal dis­
covery and graph editing techniques in combination with ML algorithms
specifically designed for causal effect estimation. Approaches such as
meta-learners and double ML [55,80,81], which incorporate data de-
biasing mechanisms, offer promising directions for more accurate causal
effect estimation.
Finally, while our contributions focus on the data center domain,
we derive domain knowledge from a simulated testbed and two real
operational data centers, using descriptions of the physical systems, the
deployed sensors, and available schematics or P&IDs. Nevertheless, we
believe that the proposed framework and methods could also be applied
to other energy systems. For each use case, features can be obtained
automatically through causal discovery, while domain knowledge must
be derived from the information available for the specific domain, and
does not necessarily have to originate from the same sources used for
data centers. Future work could address this by evaluating the proposed
methods on other energy systems and assessing their advantages and
challenges, such as more limited domain knowledge, higher sampling
resolutions, or a larger number of variables.
6 . Conclusions
Motivated by the need for more sustainable data centers and the lim­
its of purely data-driven modelling of their operations, we proposed and
evaluated the TempCaFe framework for selecting causal features based
on causal discovery algorithms and human domain knowledge. Our ex­
perimental findings not only suggest that the identified causal feature
sets improve prediction performance, especially in interventional set­
tings, but also require less training data (both in terms of features and
samples) and are easier to interpret due to their grounding in causal
knowledge of the system under investigation. Overall, our study high­
lights the value of integrating causal inference and domain knowledge
with flexible ML algorithms to improve prediction and decision-making
in energy systems like data centers.

Appendix B . Water-cooled testbed (MiniDC)
To rigorously assess data-driven modelling of physical systems, researchers emphasize the necessity of controlled environments where the un­
derlying dynamics are well understood [89,90]. While simulations offer useful insights, they cannot fully substitute for real-world experimentation.
Motivated by these ideas, we developed a water-cooled data center testbed integrated with a district heating network. The testbed has sensors and
programmable actuators; this setup allows us to conduct precise interventions and gather high-resolution time-series data. The experiments with
the testbed allow for forecasting the waste heat potential, quantified by using as a proxy the temperature of water circulating through the heating
system, and evaluating the predictive accuracy of the models after interventions.
The testbed’s P&ID is shown in Fig. B.13. It has two sub-systems: the DC side and the residential building side, each with its own water circuit.
On the DC side, the pipeline starts at a heat exchanger (HEX) connected to one Raspberry Pi (Pi), flows to a second HEX on another Pi, and then goes
into a water-to-water HEX. At this point, the water temperature is recorded by transmitter TT1. This HEX passes waste heat from the DC loop to the
residential loop. Afterward, the water temperature is measured again with TT2, then cooled in a water-to-air HEX with a fan, and finally returns to
the tank before being pumped back to the Pis. In this loop, the CPUs of the Pis act as the heat source, and cooling is done through the water-to-water
HEX or the water-to-air HEX with the fan. We also installed an outdoor air temperature transmitter (TT4), a pressure sensor (PT1), and a humidity

Appendix C . Water-cooled data center (DC1)
The water-cooled DC provides public cloud services, including Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) and managed Kubernetes servers. It consists of
seven racks, each equipped with around 48 heat exchangers, and direct-chip cooling dedicated to individual CPUs. At the base of each rack is a
coolant distribution unit, which manages the flow of cooling fluid.
The primary heat exchanger at the bottom of each rack receives water at temperatures between 35◦C and 55◦C and returns it at elevated
temperatures ranging from 45◦C up to 60◦C. The cooling system for this heated water is structured around three heat exchanger configurations. The
first transfers excess heat to the return water of the building’s heating system for heat recovery, which supplies thermal energy to nearby facilities

third relies on water chilled by mechanical chillers located on the rooftop. The cooling systems are activated in the following sequence to maximize
energy efficiency, reduce electricity consumption, and increase the reuse of waste heat: heat recovery, free cooling, then chiller-based cooling. The
recovered heat represents about 40%. A diagram of one water-cooled rack can be seen in Fig. C.15.

Appendix F . Sensitivity analysis of causal discovery thresholds
Causal discovery algorithms rely on important hyperparameters, such as the significance threshold (𝛼-value) used as a cutoff for the variable-lag
selection. Lower values lead to more stringent feature selection, resulting in fewer selected features, whereas higher values select more features. In
the main experiments, an 𝛼-value of 0.01 was used. When combined with Algorithm  1 and domain knowledge, this threshold was relaxed to 0.05.
In this Appendix, we evaluate the effect of varying this important threshold as a sensitivity analysis. We focus on the PCMCI causal discovery
method combined with an MLP learning algorithm, as this approach is competitive in terms of predictive performance on the complete test set and
after interventions. Moreover, the MLP supports both the select lag and all lags strategies. We evaluate these models across all datasets while varying
the 𝛼-value from 0.001 up to 0.1.

Appendix G . Ablation analysis of the degradation of domain knowledge
The domain knowledge (DK) graph does not necessarily represent the true causal structure of the physical system, as no ground-truth causal
graph is available for a data center. Instead, it is an approximation derived from expert knowledge and may therefore contain inaccuracies. In this
Appendix, we evaluate how the degradation of the domain knowledge graph affects model performance.
For this analysis, we use a dataset from the MiniDC, due to the well-known dynamics of the testbed, and combine PCMCI with an MLP using the
selected lag strategy. We evaluate the prediction performance after interventions while progressively degrading the quality of the domain knowledge
graph. Specifically, we first consider the full domain knowledge graph, in which all causal variables are connected to the target variable and its (a
total of 5). We then systematically remove variables from the domain knowledge graph one by one.
Fig. G.21 shows the results. It can be seen that DK&CDL_PCMCI (using variables from domain knowledge and lags from causal discovery) achieves
the best performance when the complete domain knowledge graph is available, but its performance degrades systematically as variables are removed.
In contrast, DK&CDV_PCMCI (using variables from both domain knowledge and causal discovery, with lags from the former) performs between the
original PCMCI and DK&CDL_PCMCI and also degrades as the domain knowledge graph is reduced. However, when the domain knowledge becomes
very poor (i.e., only one variable remains), DK&CDL_PCMCI continues to degrade, whereas DK&CDV_PCMCI stabilizes and achieves a performance
similar to PCMCI alone.
These results indicate that using only domain knowledge variables (DK&CDL_PCMCI) can yield the best performance when the causal graph
is accurate, but its performance deteriorates rapidly as the quality of the domain knowledge decreases, eventually becoming worse than using
causal discovery alone. On the other hand, DK&CDV_PCMCI combines the strengths of domain knowledge and causal discovery and degrades more
gracefully when the domain knowledge is imperfect. Therefore, if reliable domain knowledge of the physical system is available, DK&CDL_PCMCI
may be preferred. However, when the correctness of the domain knowledge graph is uncertain, DK&CDV_PCMCI is the more robust and preferable
approach.
